Two more gotchas: a transition needs the animated property to have a defined baseline value to interpolate *from* (animating to/from `auto` height doesn't work — you need an explicit value or a different technique), and a transition fires on *state change*, so a bare `transition` with no changing target simply does nothing visible.
sections.summary: Transitions smooth the jump between a baseline utility and a state variant like `hover:scale-105`; stick to `transform`/`opacity`/`filter` for 60fps, avoid animating layout properties, and gate motion behind `motion-safe:`/`motion-reduce:` for accessibility.

variants.question: A card should smoothly grow slightly on hover. Which combination produces a 60fps-friendly effect?
options: `transition-transform duration-200 hover:scale-105` on the card element
`transition-all duration-200 hover:w-[105%] hover:h-[105%]` on the card
`hover:scale-105` alone, relying on the browser to animate the scale by default
`transition duration-200 hover:mx-2 hover:my-2` to enlarge the card via margins
variants.rationale: `hover:scale-105` sets the end state (a `transform`), and `transition-transform duration-200` smooths the change. Transforms are GPU-composited and don't trigger layout or paint, so the growth animates at 60fps. Animating `w`/`h` or margins would recompute layout every frame (janky), and a bare `hover:scale-105` with no `transition` would snap instantly rather than animate.
optionExplanations: Correct — a `transform` end-state plus `transition-transform` gives GPU-composited, layout-free 60fps growth.
`hover:w-*`/`hover:h-*` animate layout dimensions, forcing per-frame layout recomputation — the janky path this app's invariant forbids.
Without a `transition` utility the scale change applies instantly — there's no default animation, so it snaps rather than smoothly grows.
Animating margins is a layout change (reflows siblings every frame) and doesn't even scale the card — wrong mechanism and janky.
variants.interviewTip: Reach for `transform` and `opacity` for any hover motion. Saying 'transforms are composited so they don't trigger layout or paint' names the exact reason they hit 60fps while animating width doesn't — a performance answer with a mechanism behind it.

variants.question: A developer writes `transition-transform duration-300` on a button but sees no animation at all when interacting with it. What is the most likely reason?
options: `transition-transform` must be paired with `transition-colors` before either declaration takes any effect
There's no changing target — no `hover:`/`focus:` variant alters a transform, so nothing interpolates
`duration-300` is below the browser's minimum animation threshold, so the transition is silently dropped
Transitions require an explicit `will-change: transform` utility or they never actually run on the element
variants.rationale: A transition only animates when a property actually *changes* value. `transition-transform duration-300` declares that transforms should animate over 300ms — but if no state variant (`hover:scale-105`, `focus:rotate-3`, etc.) ever changes the transform, there's nothing to interpolate and the button sits still. The fix is adding the end-state variant that the transition is meant to smooth.
optionExplanations: Transition properties are independent — `transition-transform` works alone; it doesn't need `transition-colors` present to function.
Correct — a transition needs a value change to animate; with no variant altering the transform, there's nothing to interpolate.
300ms is a normal, well-above-threshold duration — there's no minimum that would silently drop it; the missing piece is a changing value.
`will-change` is a performance hint, not a requirement — transitions run without it; the real gap is the absent state change.
variants.interviewTip: Debug transitions by asking 'what value is actually changing?' A `transition-*` with no state variant to smooth is inert. Naming that the transition needs a start *and* a different end value shows you understand interpolation, not just the syntax.

variants.question: An accessibility review flags a persistent `animate-bounce` icon for users who set 'reduce motion.' Which Tailwind approach correctly respects that preference?
options: Wrap the icon in JavaScript that removes the class after a couple of seconds so the motion eventually stops
Gate it with `motion-safe:animate-bounce` so it animates only when the user hasn't requested reduced motion
Lower the animation to `animate-pulse`, which is exempt from the reduced-motion preference by design
Leave `animate-bounce` in place but add `duration-1000` so the slower motion satisfies the accessibility rule
variants.rationale: `motion-safe:*` applies a utility only when `prefers-reduced-motion` is *not* set, so `motion-safe:animate-bounce` animates for everyone else and stays completely still for users who requested reduced motion. It maps directly onto the media query the preference exposes — the correct, declarative way to honor it (the mirror variant `motion-reduce:*` applies rules only when reduction *is* requested).
optionExplanations: Auto-stopping after a delay still plays motion the user asked to avoid — it doesn't respect the preference, it just shortens the violation.
Correct — `motion-safe:animate-bounce` runs the animation only when reduced motion is *not* requested, honoring the preference.
No animation utility is 'exempt' — `animate-pulse` is still motion and still needs gating; swapping the animation doesn't respect the preference.
Slowing motion isn't the same as removing it — a user who requested reduced motion should see none, so `duration-1000` still fails the check.
variants.interviewTip: `prefers-reduced-motion` is a real accessibility requirement, not a nicety. Knowing `motion-safe:` / `motion-reduce:` — and that the reduced-motion state needs a usable *static* end-state, not just slower motion — signals you build inclusive UI by default.

variants.question: A panel with `transition-all duration-300` won't animate open when its height goes from `h-0` to `h-auto` on toggle. Why does the height transition fail, and what's the usual fix?
options: `transition-all` excludes height by design; switch to an explicit `transition-[height]` to opt height in
The browser can't interpolate to `auto`, since it's not a resolvable numeric value to animate toward
`duration-300` is too short for a height change, so the panel jumps; a longer duration animates it
Height can't be transitioned at all; only `transform` and `opacity` are animatable properties in CSS
variants.rationale: A transition interpolates between two resolvable values, and `auto` isn't one — the browser has no numeric target to animate toward, so it snaps instead. The common fixes are transitioning to an explicit pixel height (often measured in JS), animating `max-height` between finite values, or using a `transform: scaleY()` / grid-rows technique instead. It's the same 'needs a defined value to interpolate' rule that also breaks animating from `auto`.
optionExplanations: `transition-all` does include height — opting height in isn't the issue; the failure is that the `auto` target isn't interpolatable.
Correct — `auto` has no resolved numeric value, so the browser can't interpolate toward it and the height simply snaps.
Duration doesn't cause the snap — any duration fails because the endpoint is `auto`; the problem is the value, not the timing.
Height *is* animatable between explicit values — it's just layout-triggering and can't animate to `auto`; the blanket claim is false.
variants.interviewTip: 'You can't transition to auto' is a classic gotcha. The mature answer names why (no resolvable endpoint) and the escape hatches — measured pixel height, `max-height`, or a `grid-template-rows: 0fr→1fr` trick — which shows real hands-on layout experience.
